6c90e05dce9e683c.description: Background Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is a key mediator of neuroplasticity and has been associated with disease progression in multiple sclerosis (MS). While aerobic exercise is consistently linked to BDNF modulation, the specific contribution of isolated resistance training (RT) remains unclear, as previous reviews have largely combined multimodal exercise interventions. Objective To systematically review and meta-analyze the effects of isolated RT on peripheral BDNF levels in individuals with MS (PROSPERO: CRD420251141069). Methods Searches were conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, Scielo, Scopus, PEDro and Cochrane up to January 10, 2026, using PICOT criteria. Controlled experimental studies investigating isolated RT and BDNF outcomes were included. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2.0 and ROBINS-I, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE. Due to methodological heterogeneity, a random-effects model was applied to estimate pooled effects. Results Four studies (three RCTs and one controlled non-randomized trial), totaling 126 participants with MS, were included. Interventions lasted 8-24 weeks, with training frequencies of 2-3 sessions per week. Meta-analytic synthesis revealed positive pooled effects (SMD = 0.49; 95%CI: 0.15 to 0.83; Z = 2.80; p Conclusion Isolated RT may increase peripheral BDNF levels in individuals with MS, but this effect is supported by limited and low-certainty evidence. Furthermore, given that only four studies were inclu
6c90e05dce9e683c.summary: A meta-analysis of four controlled studies (126 people with MS) found resistance training alone was linked to higher blood levels of BDNF, a neuroplasticity marker (SMD 0.49). The authors say the evidence is limited and low-certainty.
6c90e05dce9e683c.title: Is resistance training effective to increase BDNF in multiple sclerosis? An updated systematic review and meta-analysis of isolated interventions.

8ba3bcb143b805a8.description: Multiple sclerosis (MS) prevalence has increased to medium-to-high levels in several countries of the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), while Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) exposure as one of the most consistently reported MS risk factors is common throughout the region. This systematic review and meta-analysis descriptively mapped published estimates of MS prevalence and EBV seroprevalence alongside each other in MENA countries. We searched MEDLINE, PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science until 18 June 2022. Observational studies reporting MS prevalence or EBV seroprevalence among healthy MENA populations were eligible. For quantitative EBV synthesis, we restricted analyses to studies reporting VCA-IgG seroprevalence to improve comparability across studies. Studies reporting the prevalence of specific type of MS or those assessing EBV infection by IgA antibodies or non-serological tissues or without a control arm representing general population were excluded. The Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal tools were used to determine the quality of the studies. The heterogeneity of studies was evaluated using I 2 statistics. Results of the fix-effects meta-analysis were presented using prevalence and 95% confidence intervals. Of 4,323 records identified, 131 studies were included. 8ba3bcb143b805a8.summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 131 studies in the Middle East and North Africa found pooled MS prevalence of 51.02 per 100,000 and EBV VCA-IgG seroprevalence of 75%. Pooled MS prevalence rose over time, from 12 per 100,000 in the earliest period.
8ba3bcb143b805a8.title: Mapping the prevalence of Epstein-Barr virus and multiple sclerosis in Middle East and North Africa: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

acfa17cd22d3f09b.description: What are disease modifying drugs in MS? 30 August 2022 Disease modifying drugs (DMDs) are a group of treatments for people with multiple sclerosis. For people with RRMS, disease modifying drugs reduce the number of relapses you might experience as well as reducing the severity of any relapses you do have. There are a wide range of drugs approved for use by the NHS in the UK. Each drug offers a different combination of benefits and possible risks. ec61e6fd34acbfe3.summary: A Nature paper reports a multiancestry genome-wide association study of multiple sclerosis combined with multiomics analyses, examining the spatial and cellular features of MS genetics. No abstract or results were provided, so specific findings are not available.
ec61e6fd34acbfe3.title: Multiancestry genome-wide association and multiomics analyses elucidate spatiocellular features of multiple sclerosis genetics

f1b32b8e788c3f04.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising cause of age-related cognitive decline involving brain cells previously thought to be entirely beneficial. As these cells become dysfunctional, they can produce abnormal amounts of myelin, disrupting nerve fibers and potentially contributing to worsening memory and thinking skills.
f1b32b8e788c3f04.summary: Scientists report that oligodendrocytes, brain cells previously thought entirely beneficial, can become dysfunctional with age and produce abnormal amounts of myelin. This may disrupt nerve fibers and potentially contribute to worsening memory and thinking skills.
f1b32b8e788c3f04.title: Brain cells meant to protect us may be fueling cognitive decline

f40769728b6dec4c.title: Predicting follow-up cognition using estimated structural and functional connectivity networks and artificial intelligence in multiple sclerosis

f5815cad7cae3e07.description: Background Tolebrutinib is an oral, brain-penetrant Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor being investigated for multiple sclerosis (MS). Early data point to reduced relapse rates and radiological disease activity, along with a reassuring safety profile. This systematic review and meta-analysis bring together the available evidence on its clinical efficacy and adverse events. Methods We searched PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus through February 2026 using predefined eligibility criteria. Data were extracted on efficacy outcomes (disability progression and improvement, MRI activity, and brain volume change) and safety outcomes (any adverse events, serious adverse events, adverse events leading to discontinuation, headache, ALT elevation, and death). Continuous outcomes were pooled as means using reported means and standard deviations; proportional outcomes were pooled from event and total counts. Analyses were run in R using random-effects models, with data unsuitable for pooling described narratively. Results Four publications met our inclusion criteria: three reporting four randomized controlled trials and one long-term extension study. Tolebrutinib reduced the risk of confirmed disability progression at both ≥3 and ≥6 months, and disability improvement at 6 months was numerically higher than with comparators, though not conclusively so. f5815cad7cae3e07.summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of four publications (four randomized trials plus one extension study) found tolebrutinib reduced confirmed disability progression at 3 and 6 months. Disability improvement was numerically higher than with comparators, though not conclusively so.
f5815cad7cae3e07.title: Efficacy and safety of tolebrutinib in multiple sclerosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

f5a81ac2ed32e5a6.summary: A recent study found that pain in people with MS was associated with more reported difficulties with thinking and memory, but did not predict performance on objective cognition tests. Mental health issues, pain and fatigue were linked to greater perceived cognitive problems.
f5a81ac2ed32e5a6.title: Pain linked to perceived cognitive difficulties in MS study

f69c53d3129b59db.description: Hypertension begins harming the brain surprisingly early, even before measurable blood pressure increases. Key cells related to blood vessels, signaling, and myelin maintenance begin aging prematurely and malfunctioning. These disruptions resemble early patterns seen in cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s. Encouragingly, losartan reversed some of this early damage in mice.
f69c53d3129b59db.summary: A study found hypertension begins harming the brain before blood pressure measurably rises, with cells tied to blood vessels, signaling, and myelin maintenance aging prematurely. The changes resemble early cognitive decline patterns, and losartan reversed some damage in mice.
f69c53d3129b59db.title: Your brain shows damage before your blood pressure even rises
